TITLE: The Impacts of Natural Disasters on Educational Attainment: Cross-Country Evidence from Macro Data
JOURNAL_OR_SOURCE: USF Scholarship Repository (University of San Francisco)
FULL_TEXT_REASON: Endogeneity concerns and unverified exogeneity of disaster exposure
ASSESSMENT_NOTES: The study uses a panel of 85 countries from 1960 to 1990, Barro-Lee educational-attainment data, country and year fixed effects, and robust standard errors. It nevertheless assumes that natural disasters are exogenous and acknowledges that economic-damage measures create endogeneity. The macro-country design cannot fully isolate causal effects and may be affected by measurement error, omitted variables and heterogeneous data quality. It is useful for discussing shocks and long-run educational dynamics, but causal claims require caution.

TITLE: Female Enrollment, Child Mortality and Corruption Are Good Predictors of a Country’s UN Education Index.
FULL_TEXT_REASON: Non-nested feature selection and optimistically biased cross-validation
ASSESSMENT_NOTES: The study analyzes 165 countries and 47 candidate predictors averaged over 2012-2017. Predictors were first filtered using full-sample univariate R-squared values and missingness thresholds. LASSO was then applied using the complete sample, and leave-one-out cross-validation was applied only after the final variables had been selected. Because filtering and LASSO selection were not repeated inside each training fold, the reported out-of-sample R-squared of 0.8936 is exposed to selection leakage and optimistic bias. Three countries were removed because of missing GNI data. No imputation strategy, nested cross-validation, simple baseline, bootstrap selection stability analysis, or reproducible code repository was identified. The article is useful for discussing indicator selection and validation limitations, but its predictive result should not be compared directly with externally grouped validation.

TITLE: How Different are Immigrants? A Cross-Country and Cross-Survey Analysis of Educational Achievement
FULL_TEXT_REASON: Descriptive cross-survey comparison with selection and comparability limitations
ASSESSMENT_NOTES: The study compares immigrant and native student achievement using PISA, TIMSS and PIRLS. Its cross-survey comparison is informative and tests whether patterns are robust across assessments. However, survey target populations, subjects, ages and sampling designs differ; response-rate problems are noted for some countries; immigrant selection is not causally resolved; and the main regression analyses are descriptive OLS models. The study is suitable as contextual evidence but not as a causal estimate of immigrant status.

TITLE: Strategic management of equity in early childhood education: A mathematical framework with clustering, inequality metrics, and system dynamics
JOURNAL_OR_SOURCE: International Journal of Research Studies in Management
FULL_TEXT_REASON: Severe complete-case selection and aggregated dynamic design
ASSESSMENT_NOTES: The study is relevant because it uses UNESCO UIS indicators, hierarchical clustering, Gini and Theil indices, and an AR(1) model with a COVID-19 structural-break dummy. However, only 16 of 210 countries or territories were retained because of data completeness, creating severe selection risk. Global trends are based on this restricted sample, the AR(1) is estimated on aggregated averages rather than a country panel, and the steady state is an algebraic property rather than evidence of structural educational equilibrium. The study may support methods and limitations but not global inference.

TITLE: Within-School Wealth Inequality and Learning Achievement: Evidence From PISA
FULL_TEXT_REASON: Methodologically adequate multi-cycle PISA inequality study
ASSESSMENT_NOTES: The study uses PISA 2012, 2015, and 2018, two-level mixed-effects models, country fixed effects, sampling weights, replicate weights, plausible values, and robustness checks using reading outcomes, larger schools, and alternative inequality measures. It reconstructs the 2012 wealth index using the later two-parameter IRT approach for cross-cycle consistency. Important limitations remain: the analysis is observational and does not identify causality; treatment of all plausible values and variance pooling should be confirmed in the published version and annexes; missing-data handling is not fully documented; and no code repository or replication package was identified. The Research Square preprint was used for assessment, but the final citation must use the 2025 Review of Income and Wealth article, DOI 10.1111/roiw.70040.

TITLE: Performance decline in a low‐stakes test at age 15 and educational attainment at age 25: Cross‐country longitudinal evidence
AUTHORS: Francesca Borgonovi; Alessandro Ferrara; M. Piacentini
ASSESSMENT_NOTES: The study links PISA 2000 or 2003 participants to longitudinal outcomes at ages 25 to 27 in Australia, Denmark, and Switzerland. It applies PISA sampling and replication weights, combines them with longitudinal follow-up weights, clusters standard errors by school, models item and booklet effects, and reports robustness checks. Important limitations include attrition of 36 percent response in Australia and 44 percent in Denmark, limited country diversity, different PISA major domains, and an associational rather than causal design.

TITLE: Факторы, влияющие на достижения Казахстанских учащихся в международном исследовании PISA-2018
AUTHORS: Оспанова Улжан Абаевна; K. Nurumov; M. Atanaeva
FULL_TEXT_REASON: Adequate multilevel PISA analysis using plausible values and complex sample design
ASSESSMENT_NOTES: The study evaluates mathematics, reading and science achievement among Kazakhstani students using PISA 2018. It explicitly reports multilevel regression analysis, plausible values and complex sample-design procedures, and separates individual, school and regional factors. It remains an observational single-country analysis and does not identify causal effects. Missing-data treatment and replication materials are not sufficiently clear, but the methodological alignment with PISA makes it a final candidate.

TITLE: EduForecast: A Comparative AI Model for Predicting Global Education Performance through XGBoost and Random Forest Intelligence
AUTHORS: Jose C. Agoylo; Lykzelle Mae C. Padasas; Gardenia B. Concillo; Jimson A. Olaybar; Alex C. Bacalla
FULL_TEXT_REASON: Target leakage and inadequate validation design
ASSESSMENT_NOTES: Enrollment Rate is the target, but the predictors include Literacy-to-Enrollment Ratio and Enrollment-literacy gap, both of which mathematically contain the target. The study also uses a random 80-20 split without grouping by country or year, reports inconsistent R2 values between table and figure, provides no simple baseline, and does not provide code or sufficient dataset coverage information.

TITLE: Education for Growth: Why and For Whom?
FULL_TEXT_REASON: Strong methodological analysis of measurement error and heterogeneity in education-growth models
ASSESSMENT_NOTES: The study compares Barro-Lee, Kyriacou and World Values Survey education measures and demonstrates severe attenuation from measurement error in first-differenced country data. It evaluates alternative time windows, instrumental variables, capital controls, non-linearity and heterogeneous country coefficients. It explicitly warns that reverse causality and omitted policies prevent simple causal interpretation. The careful treatment of measurement error and specification sensitivity makes it a strong methodological reference.

TITLE: Decentralization and the quality of public services: Cross-country evidence from educational data
JOURNAL_OR_SOURCE: Environment and Planning C Politics and Space
FULL_TEXT_REASON: Incomplete PISA design treatment and uncertain instrument validity
ASSESSMENT_NOTES: The study uses four PISA waves for 22 countries, country and year fixed effects, multilevel models, and instrumental-variable estimators. It recognizes the five plausible values and tests endogeneity, weak identification, underidentification, and overidentifying restrictions. However, the reviewed text does not establish correct use of final sampling weights, replicate weights, or repeated estimation and pooling across plausible values. The proposed instruments may directly affect educational outcomes through urbanization, resources, or population structure. Results should not be treated as definitive causal effects.

TITLE: Education Expenditure and Access to Education: Case Study of United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization Declaration in Nigeria
AUTHORS: Bassey Okon Ebi; Peter Samuel Ubi
JOURNAL_OR_SOURCE: International Journal of Economics and Financial Issues
FULL_TEXT_REASON: Unsupported causal claims and inadequate time-series design
ASSESSMENT_NOTES: The analysis uses only 26 annual observations and 24 observations in Granger tests. It does not document unit-root, stationarity, cointegration, or error-correction analysis. The projected education-expenditure variable is deterministically constructed as 26 percent of total expenditure and is not an observed policy treatment. Nominal trends, limited controls, and unsupported causal interpretations create major risk of spurious results. The claimed UNESCO 26 percent benchmark is supported only through secondary references and must not be treated as an official UNESCO recommendation without a primary source.

TITLE: Who Makes It Into PISA? Understanding the Impact of PISA Sample Eligibility Using Turkey as a Case Study (PISA 2003 - PISA 2012)
FULL_TEXT_REASON: Strong analysis of PISA eligibility, coverage and changing sample composition
ASSESSMENT_NOTES: The OECD study examines Turkey across PISA 2003 to 2012 and shows that eligibility rose from approximately 45 percent to 80 percent. It combines PISA and Demographic and Health Survey data, uses survey weighting, five plausible values, composite standard errors and multiple robustness checks. The study directly demonstrates how changing sample coverage can bias trend interpretation. It is limited to one national case and does not estimate a causal intervention effect, but it is essential for interpreting international assessment trends.

TITLE: Functional literacy, educational attainment and earnings : a multi-country comparison
AUTHORS: Kevin Denny; Colm Harmon; Vincent O’Sullivan
FULL_TEXT_REASON: Inadequate plausible-value treatment and potential earnings-sample selection
ASSESSMENT_NOTES: The study uses International Adult Literacy Survey data, population weights, interval-regression methods for banded earnings and robust standard errors. It finds that literacy is associated with earnings across countries. However, it averages plausible values to construct literacy scores rather than estimating and pooling across plausible values. The working sample excludes individuals without usable earnings observations, creating selection risk, and causal identification is absent. It is useful with major limitations.

TITLE: Predictive Modeling of Educational Outcomes Using Machine Learning for Data-Driven Regional Education Policy
FULL_TEXT_REASON: Outcome-predictor circularity and inadequate external validation
ASSESSMENT_NOTES: The regional education score is a composite of attainment and post-secondary measures, while dominant predictors include Level 3 achievement at age 18, attainment variables, and higher-education participation. This creates potential construct overlap and target leakage. The random 80-20 split does not separate regions or years, no simple baseline is reported, and the claimed R2 of 0.9881 is not supported by external, spatial, or temporal validation.
